tagline: Rift Valley city on the shore of a flamingo-fringed soda lake, gateway to Kenya's classic safari circuit.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are not metered; agree on a fare before starting the ride, or use a ride-hailing app for a fixed, transparent price.

emergency.note: 112 works on all mobile networks and connects to police, fire, and ambulance; response outside major towns can be slow.

hood_desc: An upscale, leafy residential area on Nakuru's western edge with spacious compounds and government residences; suits travelers wanting a quiet base close to town.
The bustling commercial core around Kenyatta Avenue and the CBD, with shops, banks, and markets; best for first-time visitors who want everything walkable.
The forested, fenced sanctuary just south of town famed for its flamingo-lined soda lake, rhino sanctuary, and lodges; the main reason most travelers come to Nakuru.
An older, working-class neighborhood near the historic Bondeni Market with cheap eats and everyday local life; suits budget travelers wanting an authentic feel.
A lively strip of bars, nyama choma joints, and food stalls popular for evening socializing; good for travelers wanting nightlife and casual dining.

transit.hours: Matatus and boda bodas run roughly 5:30 AM to 10 PM; limited service after dark for safety reasons.
transit.pay: Cash paid directly to the conductor (tout) or driver; fares are informal and can vary, so confirm the price before boarding.
transit.note: Nakuru has no formal metro, tram, or commuter rail; matatus, boda bodas, and tuk-tuks are the main ways to get around, supplemented by ride-hailing apps in town.

train: Nairobi-Kisumu meter-gauge railway (limited passenger service through Nakuru)
bus: Matatu routes to Nairobi, Eldoret, Kisumu
Easy Coach and Modern Coast intercity buses

tip.r: Not expected in local eateries, but 10% is appreciated at tourist-oriented restaurants and lodges; tipping safari guides and drivers (a few dollars per day) is customary.

tagline: Desert oasis capital of Peru's pisco and wine country, minutes from the palm-ringed Huacachina lagoon.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are unmetered; agree on the fare before getting in, or use a ride-hailing app for a fixed price.

emergency.note: 116 is the fire brigade (Bomberos); response times outside Lima can be slower, especially at night.

hood_desc: Ica's colonial-era heart, anchored by the cathedral and the Museo Regional de Ica's Paracas and Nazca artifacts; best for first-time visitors who want sights and dining within walking distance.
A palm-ringed desert lagoon minutes from downtown, surrounded by towering dunes and famed for dune-buggy rides and sandboarding; suits adventure travelers chasing sunset views.
A quiet traditional neighborhood tied to local legends of witches (brujas), with small family-run eateries; good for travelers wanting an authentic, low-key feel.
A rural district on Ica's outskirts home to pisco and wine bodegas like El Catador, with tasting tours through vineyards; suits travelers interested in Peru's pisco heritage.
Countryside district holding Bodega Tacama, one of the oldest wineries in South America, amid vineyards and open desert scenery; good for wine tourism and a slower pace.

transit.hours: Mototaxis and combis run roughly 6 AM to 10-11 PM; taxis and ride apps cover late night.
transit.pay: Cash paid directly to the driver; mototaxi fares are negotiated and combis charge a fixed per-route amount, generally 1-3 soles within the city.
transit.note: Ica has no metro or formal bus network; mototaxis are the primary way to get around, with combis linking Ica to Huacachina and surrounding towns.

bus: Cruz del Sur, Oltursa, and other intercity buses to Lima and Nazca

tip.r: Not obligatory; some restaurants add a 10% service charge automatically, in which case an extra tip isn't expected, otherwise rounding up or 10% is appreciated.

tagline: Denmark's youthful second city, blending Viking-age roots with student energy and harborfront modernism.

taxi.fareNote: All taxis are metered with regulated fares; ride-hailing apps are also available, but licensed taxis remain common and reliable.

emergency.note: 112 connects to police, fire, and ambulance for emergencies; 114 is for non-urgent police matters.

hood_landmark.Latinerkvarteret (Latin Quarter): Vor Frue Kirke (Church of Our Lady), Aarhus

hood_desc: Aarhus's compact historic core around the cathedral, pedestrian shopping streets, and the harbor front; best for first-time visitors who want everything walkable.
A maze of cobbled medieval lanes filled with independent boutiques, cafes, and Vor Frue Kirke; ideal for travelers who enjoy browsing small shops and old-town charm.
A striking modern waterfront district built on former docklands, anchored by the Dokk1 library/culture house and the Iceberg apartment complex; suits architecture fans and photographers.
A trendy, tree-lined residential quarter south of downtown known for cafes, natural wine bars, and independent shops; popular with young locals and digital nomads.
A quieter university district near Aarhus University and the Botanical Garden; suits travelers wanting a calmer, green base close to museums.

transit.hours: Buses and light rail run roughly 5 AM to midnight, with a reduced night bus network on weekends.
transit.pay: Pay with a Rejsekort contactless card or the DOT/Midttrafik mobile ticket app; single tickets can also be bought via app or at stops.
transit.note: Aarhus's light rail (Letbanen) connects the city center to the northern and southern suburbs, complementing an extensive bus network; the city center itself is highly walkable and bike-friendly.

air: Billund Airport (~90 km, more international routes)
train: DSB InterCity trains to Copenhagen, Aalborg, Esbjerg

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus to city center (~45 min)

tip.r: Service charges are already included in prices by law; tipping is not customary, though rounding up or leaving small change for excellent service is appreciated.

tagline: Benin's quiet official capital of royal palaces, Vodun heritage, and lagoon calm, overshadowed by bustling Cotonou.

taxi.fareNote: Almost all rides are by zemidjan (motorcycle taxi) or shared taxi with no meters; agree on the price in CFA francs before setting off.

emergency.note: 118 reaches the fire brigade; response times can be slow outside the city center, so hotels and clinics are often the fastest first call.

hood_desc: Home to the National Assembly and the Ethnographic Museum's Yoruba masks and royal artifacts; the natural first stop for understanding Beninese and Yoruba history.
A leafy colonial-era plaza with a statue of Porto-Novo's first king, ringed by administrative buildings; a calm spot to get oriented near the center.
The historic royal quarter around King Toffa's Palace (Honmé Museum), on UNESCO's tentative list; suits travelers focused on Beninese royal and Vodun heritage.
A quiet residential district built by returning Afro-Brazilian former slaves, known for Portuguese-style facades and the Da Silva Museum of Beninese-Brazilian history.
The working port and market district on the lagoon, where canoes and zemidjans converge around Porto-Novo's largest market; best for travelers wanting an authentic, unpolished feel.

transit.hours: No fixed schedule; zemidjans and shared taxis run informally from early morning to late evening, thinning out after dark.
transit.pay: Cash only (CFA francs), negotiated per ride before departing; there is no fare card or ticketing system.
transit.note: Porto-Novo has no formal public transit network. Zemidjans (motorcycle taxis) are the main way to get around the city, supplemented by shared taxis and bush taxis to Cotonou and other towns; canoes still cross the lagoon to nearby villages.

bus: Shared taxis/bush taxis to Cotonou and regional towns
ferry: Lagoon canoe (pirogue) crossings to nearby lakeside villages

tip.r: Not part of local custom; rounding up small amounts is appreciated at tourist-oriented restaurants and hotels but never expected.

tagline: Belgium's canal-laced university city of medieval towers, vegetarian cuisine, and student energy.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are metered with regulated rates; most rides are booked by phone, app, or picked up at a taxi stand rather than hailed on the street.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU number reaching police, fire, and ambulance; 101 is the direct Belgian police line.

hood_desc: A maze of narrow medieval streets just north of Gravensteen castle, packed with some of Ghent's best restaurants and bars in restored gabled houses; ideal for food lovers who want to be steps from the main sights.
The pedestrianized heart of Ghent around the Belfry, Saint Bavo's Cathedral, and the Graslei/Korenlei waterfront; the natural base for first-timers who want everything walkable.
The lively student strip near Ghent University's main campus, lined with bars and late-night venues; suits younger travelers who want an energetic, budget-friendly nightlife scene.
A historic market square once the site of public gatherings and executions, now ringed by cafes, breweries, and independent shops; good for travelers who enjoy markets and craft-beer culture.
A quieter, redeveloped waterfront district along the old docks, with a marina, parks, and new housing; suits travelers seeking a calmer, residential feel away from the tourist core.

transit.hours: Trams and buses generally run from about 5:00 AM to midnight, with a limited weekend night-bus network filling the gap.
transit.pay: Pay with a rechargeable De Lijn card, the De Lijn app, or contactless bank card tap-in on trams and buses; single paper tickets bought on board cost more.
transit.note: Ghent's compact center is best explored on foot or by bike; De Lijn trams and buses cover the wider city, and Gent-Sint-Pieters station links to Brussels and beyond by rail.

transit.m: Direct train to Gent-Sint-Pieters (~50 min, hourly)

tip.r: Service is included by law in restaurant and cafe bills; rounding up or leaving about 5-10% for good service is appreciated but not expected.

tagline: Sun-soaked gateway to the Black Forest, a Gothic university city built on solar energy and easygoing charm.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis use standardized metered fares set by the local tariff board; ranks are common at the station and old town, and phone/app booking is typical.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide number for fire and medical emergencies and also reaches police; 110 is the direct German police line.

hood_desc: The compact medieval old town around Freiburg Minster, laced with trickling Bächle water runnels; the obvious base for first-time visitors with everything walkable.
A pioneering car-reduced eco-district of solar homes and the famous Solar Settlement, built on a former French military base; popular with sustainability-minded travelers and families.
An elegant, leafy residential quarter of Belle Epoque villas south of the center, home to the Colombischlössle museum and a relaxed cafe scene; suits travelers wanting a quieter, upscale base.
A mixed residential and student district near the main train station, with affordable eateries and a multicultural feel; convenient for arrivals by rail.
A quiet hillside neighborhood below the Schlossberg with vineyard paths and views over the city; good for travelers who want nature and calm close to downtown.

transit.hours: Trams and buses run roughly 4:30 AM to around 1:00 AM, with a weekend Nachtbus night network on Friday and Saturday nights.
transit.pay: Tickets from the RVF regional fare network cover trams and buses; buy from machines, the VAG/Freiburg app, or as a rechargeable card, with contactless bank card tap-in increasingly common.
transit.note: Freiburg's Stadtbahn tram network is one of the most extensive per capita in Germany and, together with an extensive bike-path network, makes a car largely unnecessary in the city.

air: Frankfurt Airport (FRA, ~220 km via ICE train)

transit.m: Airport bus/shuttle to Freiburg Hauptbahnhof (~50 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory since service is included, but rounding up or adding roughly 5-10% for good service is customary; tips are usually handed directly to the server rather than left on the table.

tagline: Danube fortress city of student energy, Habsburg streets, and Europe's biggest music festival.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered and cheap by Western standards; confirm the meter is running or agree a price beforehand, especially from the bus or train station.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-style number that reaches police, fire, and ambulance and is increasingly recommended, especially for foreigners.

hood_desc: Novi Sad's pedestrian-friendly historic core around Freedom Square, the Name of Mary Church, and City Hall; best for first-time visitors who want museums, cafes, and nightlife all within walking distance.

The fortress town across the Danube, home to the massive Petrovaradin Fortress and clock tower and the site of the EXIT Festival each July; suits history lovers and festival-goers wanting river views and cobblestone streets.
A leafy 1960s-80s district of university buildings, parks, and the Štrand river beach along the Danube; good for families, students, and travelers wanting green space and a quieter pace.
A modern business and shopping district south of downtown with malls, offices, and newer apartment blocks; suits travelers who prioritize shopping and contemporary conveniences over historic charm.

A traditional low-rise neighborhood turned canvas for street art and murals, with a growing cluster of galleries and indie cafes; suits younger travelers and art enthusiasts wanting an authentic, less touristy feel.

transit.hours: Buses generally run from about 4:30-5:00 AM until around midnight; there is no dedicated night network.
transit.pay: Fares are paid with a prepaid rechargeable BusPlus card tapped on boarding, or a slightly higher cash fare paid to the driver.
transit.note: 21 urban and 35 suburban lines are operated by the public company JGSP Novi Sad; the city's old tram network was decommissioned in 1957 and never replaced.

air: No airport in Novi Sad itself; nearest is Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport (BEG)
train: Regional trains toward Subotica and Hungary
bus: Intercity buses from Novi Sad Bus Station

transit.m: Bus/shuttle plus onward bus or train to Novi Sad

tip.r: Not expected but rounding up or leaving 5-10% at restaurants for good service is appreciated.

tagline: Cradle of Russian statehood, its Kremlin and river churches predating Moscow itself.

taxi.fareNote: Most rides are booked and priced through Yandex Go or similar apps rather than hailed on the street; agree the fare upfront if flagging a private car.

emergency.note: 112 is toll-free from any mobile phone and connects to all emergency services, though English-speaking operators are not guaranteed.

hood_desc: The walled medieval citadel on the Sofia Side of the Volkhov River, home to St. Sophia Cathedral, the Millennium of Russia monument, and several museums; the obvious first stop for any visit and easily walkable.

The former medieval marketplace and trade quarter on the river's east bank, dotted with small stone churches and reconstructed merchant arcades; suits history and architecture fans wanting a quieter counterpart to the Kremlin side.

A mid-rise residential microdistrict along the river south of the center, mostly Soviet-era apartment blocks with everyday shops and courtyards; good for travelers wanting a calmer, local base a short walk from the sights.
A leafy riverside area built around the 12th-century Anthony Monastery and its icon museum, on the northern edge of town; suits those wanting monastic architecture away from the crowds.
The city's main pedestrian shopping boulevard near the central market and bus station, lined with shops, cafes, and everyday services; the most convenient base for errands and quick bites.

transit.hours: Buses and trolleybuses generally run from around 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM.
transit.pay: Cash paid on board to the driver or conductor; foreign-issued bank cards do not work on transit or almost anywhere else in Russia since 2022.
transit.note: The five-route trolleybus network opened in 1995, the first new trolleybus system built in Russia after the Soviet collapse.

air: No scheduled flights; nearest airport is Pulkovo (LED) in St. Petersburg, 180 km away
bus: Intercity buses to St. Petersburg and Moscow

transit.m: Intercity bus from St. Petersburg to Veliky Novgorod

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving about 10% in restaurants is common in tourist-facing places but not expected elsewhere.

tagline: Isan's gateway city, guarding the Khorat Plateau at the edge of Khao Yai's jungle.

taxi.color: no standard livery (tuk-tuks and songthaews dominate)
taxi.fareNote: Few metered taxis operate outside Bangkok; agree the fare with tuk-tuk, motorbike-taxi, or songthaew drivers before departing.

emergency.note: 112 also works from mobile phones nationwide; English-speaking operators are more likely on the Tourist Police line.

hood_desc: The moated historic core around the Thao Suranaree (Yamo) Monument and Chumphon Gate, Korat's most walkable and touristed quarter; best for first-time visitors wanting temples, the old walls, and easy orientation.
The Pho Klang Road night market area with street food stalls, bars, and budget guesthouses; suits travelers who want evening energy and cheap eats within stumbling distance of their room.
The modern commercial strip along Highway 2 anchored by malls like Terminal 21 Korat and Central Korat; good for shopping, cinemas, and international chain comforts.
A quieter, leafier zone on the city's edge around Suranaree University of Technology, with student cafes and green campus space; suits longer stays or those wanting distance from downtown traffic.
The railway quarter around Thanon Chira Junction station where the Bangkok-bound and Isan lines split, with cheap noodle shops and guesthouses catering to travelers in transit.

transit.hours: Songthaews and tuk-tuks generally operate from early morning until around 8-9 PM; there is no formal city bus network.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash; songthaews charge a low flat fare per route, while tuk-tuks and motorbike taxis are negotiated per trip.
transit.note: Korat has no metro, tram, or formal public bus system; getting around relies on songthaews, tuk-tuks, motorbike taxis, and increasingly ride-hailing apps.

air: Nakhon Ratchasima Airport has no scheduled commercial flights
Nearest major airport is Suvarnabhumi (BKK) in Bangkok, about 260 km away
train: Nakhon Ratchasima Railway Station on the Bangkok-Nong Khai/Ubon Ratchathani line
High-speed rail line to Bangkok planned for 2027
bus: Korat Bus Terminal 2, with services across Isan, to Bangkok, Laos, and the Cambodian border

ride.avail: limited, usually pre-booked for long distance

tip.r: Not customary at street food stalls or markets; rounding up or leaving small change is appreciated at restaurants, and larger hotels/restaurants often add a 10% service charge already.
